steps.scene: In stop-start town traffic, you accelerate hard into every gap and brake late for every queue.

question.prompt: What's this doing to your fuel use?

options.text: Saving fuel — you spend less time on the road
Nothing — modern engines use the same either way
Using far more fuel than driving smoothly

question.explanation: Harsh acceleration and braking waste fuel and wear the car. Smooth driving can save about 15%.

steps.title: Soft tyres cost money
steps.body: Under-inflated tyres drag on the road, so the engine works harder and burns more fuel. Check your pressures regularly.

question.prompt: Which of these makes your car burn more fuel?

options.text: Under-inflated tyres
Tyres at the pressure in the handbook
Nothing about tyres — pressure only affects grip

question.explanation: Correct pressures save fuel, make the tyres last longer and keep your stopping distance as short as it can be.

a.label: Steady 50 mph
a.body: Lower revs and less air resistance — an economical way to cover the miles.

b.label: Steady 70 mph
b.body: Uses about 15% more fuel than 50 mph over the same distance.

question.prompt: How much more fuel will you use at 70 mph than at 50 mph?

options.text: None, as long as you're in top gear
About 15% more
About 75% more

question.explanation: Air resistance climbs steeply with speed. The faster you go, the harder the engine has to work.

steps.wrongBelief: Restarting the engine uses more fuel than leaving it running while you wait.

question.prompt: You've stopped at the roadside to wait several minutes for a friend. What should you do?

options.text: Keep it idling — restarting burns more fuel
Rev it now and then to keep the battery charged
Switch off the engine

question.explanation: An idling engine burns fuel and pollutes for nothing. You mustn't leave it running unnecessarily while parked.

steps.repairNote: If you'll be stationary for a while, switch off. Leaving an engine running unnecessarily while parked is against the rules.

steps.title: Short trips, cold engine
steps.body: A cold engine runs inefficiently and pollutes more. For short trips, walking or cycling is cleaner — and often quicker.

question.prompt: Which habit does the environment the most good?

options.text: Warm the engine up by idling before you set off
Avoid making lots of short journeys
Drive short trips in a low gear

question.explanation: An engine only runs cleanly once it's warm. On a short trip it barely gets there.

steps.scene: You're doing 40 mph when the traffic lights far ahead turn red.

question.prompt: What's the greenest way to deal with it?

options.text: Ease off early, stay in gear and let the car slow
Keep your speed up, then brake firmly at the line
Speed up in case they change back to green

question.explanation: Looking well ahead lets you slow gently — often without stopping at all. Late, hard braking throws that energy away.

steps.title: Old oil and batteries
steps.body: Used engine oil and old batteries are hazardous. Never pour oil down a drain — take both to a local authority disposal site.

question.prompt: You've changed your own engine oil. What should you do with the old oil?

options.text: Pour it down a drain with plenty of water
Take it to a local authority site
Put it in your household bin

question.explanation: Oil poured down a drain pollutes rivers and harms wildlife. It's also illegal.
